newsitem.title: POLAND: Easier abortion in doubt after Polish Senate vote.
newsitem.headline: Easier abortion in doubt after Polish Senate vote.

text.p: A bid to ease Poland's restrictive anti-abortion law hung in the balance on Friday after the upper house of parliament blocked the move, which was strongly opposed by the Roman Catholic Church and Polish-born Pope John Paul.
The 100-seat Senate rejected the bill late on Thursday by 50 to 40 with two abstentions in a vote that split the two parties in the ruling left-wing coalition.

The bill, which would allow women to end pregnancies before the 12th week if they were too poor to raise a child or had other personal problems, must now return for a new vote in the 460-seat lower house, which approved it in late August.
The Cathlic church, which equates abortion with killing and led a huge campaign of letters and demonstrations to halt the measure, greeted the bill's Senate defeat with deep relief.

Recalling Pope John Paul's pained words about his homeland after the earlier vote -- when he said a country that killed its own children had no future -- Archbishop Tadeusz Goclowski gave encouragement to the Pontiff who faces surgery next week.

"Holy Father, this nation has a future, because the doors have opened to hope...for this nation which wants to save the lives of unborn children," the Gdansk archbishop told PAP news agency after the Senate vote.

The present law, passed under a pro-Catholic government after the 1989 fall of communism, allows abortion only if pregnancy threatens a woman's life or health, results from rape or incest, or when the foetus is irreparably damaged.

The liberalisation originally passed the lower house with a large majority after opponents quit the chamber to try to prevent a quorum. But analysts said a new vote could be close and the bill might at the least be considerably delayed.
To succeed it now has to be passed by a 50 percent plus one majority of deputies, in which case it goes on to President Aleksander Kwasniewski who has promised to sign it into law.

"There is still a chance the liberalisation will pass but this will require great discipline from parliamentarians who support it -- if some are not present it could fail," said Wanda Nowicka, executive director of the pro-bill Federation for Women and Family Planning.
"If this bill is passed and is properly implemented it would be very positive for women," she told Reuters.
The bill, which also provides for wider sex education and cheaper contraception, requires women to undergo counselling and a time for reflection before any abortion.
It has split the mostly Catholic Poles, though surveys suggest a majority back liberalisation, designed to reduce the number of bungled back-street abortions and other tragedies.
On Thursday all Warsaw's church bells rang out in an appeal to halt the bill while up to 10,000 opponents marched on parliament with a petition.
Abortion has become a rallying point for parties aligning themselves ahead of parliamentary elections due next September.
Senators of the Polish Peasant Party (PSL) voted against the bill, which was backed by members of its larger ruling coalition partner, the Democratic Left Alliance (SLD).
The coalition is strained as some Peasants find more in common with the pro-Church, economically populist, opposition Solidarity union than with the secular, ex-communist SLD.
The Peasants, backing demands for greater influence in government with hints they might choose a new partner after the polls, have clinched a non-aggression pact with Solidarity.
The union leader Marian Krzaklewski was present to watch that PSL senators voted as Solidarity wanted, against the bill.
